# feature engineering

assignment 4 = practice for team assignment predicting home values

linear regression fits a straight line, but relationships aren't always linear

feature engineering = transforming variables to improve prediction without needing more complicated ML models

linear regression still useful because it's interpretable

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## data

2023 ACS, Philadelphia census tracts

y = median gross rent

x = income, % renters, building age, distance to city hall

building age = 2023 - median year built

\% renters = renter households / total households \* 100

distance = `st_distance()` from city hall, convert feet to miles (/5280)

`progress = FALSE` in get_acs removes progress bars in QMD

remove missing values using `filter(!is.na())`

lm silently drops missing observations, so keep the same tracts across models

377 census tracts

### cross validation

10 folds, train on 9 and test on 1, repeat

seed = 5080, same folds for each model

RMSE = root mean square error, lower is better

model log = record of each model and its RMSE

baseline (m0): rent \~ income + pct_renters + building_age + distance

**RMSE = \$265**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# logs

use when distribution is skewed or percentage changes matter more than absolute changes

30000 -\> 60000 = +30000 (100%)

170000 -\> 200000 = +30000 (17.6%)

same dollar increase, very different proportional change

### log of x (m1)

`rent ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age + distance`

income coefficient = 502

502/100 = \$5.02

1% increase in income -\> approximately \$5 higher rent

10% increase -\> \$502 \* ln(1.10) = approx \$48

didn't improve RMSE much

log(0) = -infinity

use `log1p(x)` = log(1+x) for variables with zeros (crime counts, 311 calls)

### log of y (m2)

`log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age + distance`

| Model       | Interpretation              |
|-------------|-----------------------------|
| level-level | 1 unit x -\> b units y      |
| level-log   | 1% x -\> b/100 units y      |
| log-level   | 1 unit x -\> approx 100b% y |
| log-log     | 1% x -\> approx b% y        |

log-log = elasticity

important: when logging y, RMSE is in log units

RMSE \$250 -\> 0.18 doesn't mean huge improvement

`exp(predictions)` converts predictions back to dollars before calculating RMSE

**m2 RMSE approx \$263**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# squared terms

some relationships are curved

building age vs rent:

new buildings = expensive, middle aged = cheaper, very old = desirable again (vintage)

U-shaped relationship

$$
Rent = b_0+b_1Age+b_2Age^2+\epsilon
$$

`I(building_age^2)` in R

include both age and age squared

| Linear | Squared | Shape      |
|--------|---------|------------|
| \+     | \-      | inverted U |
| \-     | \+      | U shape    |

here age negative, squared positive

### turning point

$$
x^* = \frac{-b_1}{2b_2}
$$

turning point = **76.8 years**

maximum age in data = 85 years

check that turning point is within observed range, otherwise extrapolating

ACS also groups buildings before 1940 together

**m3 RMSE = \$261**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# categorical variables

variables can already be categorical (zoning, housing type) or made into categories

example: distance to city hall

| Ring  | Distance  |
|-------|-----------|
| core  | \<2 miles |
| inner | 2-5 miles |
| outer | 5+ miles  |

`case_when()` = assign categories

`factor()` = tell R these are categories, not numbers

`cut()` = create bins from continuous variables

### dummy variables

K categories -\> K-1 dummy variables

one is the reference category

| Ring  | Coefficient |
|-------|------------:|
| core  |   reference |
| inner |        -122 |
| outer |        -164 |

inner = \$122 lower rent than core, outer = \$164 lower, holding others constant

changing reference category changes interpretation, not predictions

categorizing loses information: 2.1 and 4.9 miles both become inner

check category sizes before cross validation, otherwise some categories might be absent from training data

**m4 (distance rings) made RMSE worse**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# interactions

categories = different intercepts

interactions = different slopes

example: income might have stronger relationship with rent in core than outer ring

`log(income) * ring`

core = reference

| Ring  |    Income Slope |
|-------|----------------:|
| core  |             653 |
| inner | 653 - 219 = 434 |
| outer | 653 - 244 = 409 |

1% increase in income:

core -\> \$6.53 higher rent

inner -\> \$4.34

outer -\> \$4.09

use interactions when there's a reason to expect different relationships across groups

**m5 RMSE = \$264**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# fixed effects

some rent differences can't be explained by measured predictors

neighborhood reputation, perception, sense of place etc

fixed effects = categorical indicators capturing location-specific differences

example: Philadelphia's 18 planning districts

### spatial join

join census tracts to planning districts using `st_join(largest = TRUE)`

if tract overlaps two districts, assign it to the district with largest area of overlap

district = factor

small categories cause cross validation errors if no observations from that category are in training

professor merged small categories to have at least 10 observations per group

### model

add planning district as a categorical predictor

each district gets its own intercept adjustment

captures remaining location-specific differences, but doesn't explain exactly what causes them

can map district coefficients and compare residuals before/after

**m6 RMSE = \$256 — best model**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# model comparison

| Model | Change                          |          RMSE |
|-------|---------------------------------|--------------:|
| m0    | baseline                        |         \$265 |
| m1    | log income                      | little change |
| m2    | log rent + income               |       \~\$263 |
| m3    | squared building age            |         \$261 |
| m4    | distance categories             |         worse |
| m5    | income x ring                   |         \$264 |
| m6    | planning district fixed effects |         \$256 |

best = fixed effects

feature engineering doesn't always improve predictions

logs = proportional changes

squared = curved relationships

categories = group differences

interactions = different slopes

fixed effects = unmeasured geographic differences

**main point:** test transformations using cross-validation RMSE, not just R²
